vignette:
Kwame is a 21-year-old chef who works the evening shift at a busy downtown restaurant. He came in for an intake looking tired and guarded, his arms crossed, his eyes scanning the room. Eight months ago, after closing the restaurant, he was sexually assaulted by three men in the alley behind the building. He remembers the harsh sound of a car door slamming, then an engine idling as they cornered him. He froze completely, unable to fight back or even shout, and that paralysis has haunted him ever since.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame began noticing that ordinary sounds-a car backfiring, a truck rumbling past-would suddenly drop him back into that alley. The memories came without warning, and when they did, he would hear the car sounds in his head, as vivid as the original moment. He found himself reacting with a jolt of terror every time a customer or coworker moved abruptly near him, even when nothing was actually wrong. He started feeling on guard inside his own apartment, checking the locks twice, unable to sit still. Any sense of losing control-a crowded bus, a surprise task from his head chef-would send his heart racing and his mind straight back to the assault.

Kwame had come to believe that he acted in ways that completely violated who he was. He was certain that a stronger person-anybody else-would have fought back and stopped the assault. Because he hadn't, he felt he had no future, nothing to look forward to, no way to redeem himself. These beliefs made the triggers worse: every car sound felt like a test he was failing again. They also deepened the memories; when he tried to describe what happened to a friend, he lost the thread and couldn't finish, and the shame of that blank moment replayed the event in his head, the auditory recall sharpening.

To cope, Kwame developed strategies that now keep the cycle spinning. When a trigger like a car sound hits, he immediately starts checking his body for signs of injury-a cut, a bruise, any reminder that he is still vulnerable. At other times, he deliberately detaches from the memories, telling himself it happened to someone else, though that detachment often causes the memories to rush back even more intrusively later. He also spends hours imagining revenge on the men, replaying scenes of violence that leave him feeling more out of control and more convinced that he has lost his moral compass. The revenge fantasies themselves bring back the original memory, because they force him to re-enter the scene. His constant body monitoring and hypervigilance at home feed a looming sense of threat, which in turn makes every sudden movement in the kitchen feel like an attack, which then triggers the memory again.

At work, Kwame now avoids the alley exit, uses a different route, and has started refusing to do prep tasks that require him to stand with his back to the door. He nearly cut himself badly last week when a coworker tapped his shoulder-he spun around with a knife, his heart pounding, the full memory flooding in. What brought him to therapy was that final scare: he realized he could hurt someone or himself, and he felt a desperate need to stop the loop. He is afraid that talking about the assault will make it worse, but he is even more afraid that if he doesn't, the hopelessness will swallow him completely. After a memory surfaced in this way, even the most ordinary sound-a kettle boiling, a door clicking shut-felt like a trap he could not afford to ignore, and he would spend the next hour scanning the kitchen for any hint of danger.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not convey that the memory itself leads to or influences triggers; it only describes triggers leading to memory.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that the memory itself leads to or influences triggers; it only describes triggers leading to memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
